query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing high‐frequency laser power modulation during additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi will lower thermal gradients during solidification, thereby reducing residual stresses and suppressing elemental segregation, which together produce a refined microstructure with fewer defects and enhanced mechanical integrity compared to constant‐power processing.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with typical as-atomized morphology and a propensity for segregation and high residual stresses when processed with conventional constant laser power.
generation.intervention: Apply high-frequency modulation to the laser power during the additive manufacturing process (e.g., LPBF or DED) while maintaining a comparable overall energy density.
generation.conditions: The study will be performed on simple geometry builds (e.g., single walls or blocks) within the established AM processing window for AlCrFeNiSi. Modulation parameters (frequency and amplitude) will be varied within a range that preserves sufficient melting but introduces periodic variations in energy input, under ambient inert atmosphere and typical substrate temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined grain structure with more uniform splat formation and lower residual stress fields as well as a more homogeneous elemental distribution.
generation.mechanism: High-frequency modulation periodically adjusts the laser energy input during melting, altering the melt pool dynamics and cooling cycles. This controlled variation moderates the peak thermal gradients that drive segregation and residual stress development and helps to minimize the formation of defects such as cracks by avoiding extreme thermal conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to samples built with constant laser power, the modulated laser process is expected to yield components with reduced measured residual stress (directionally lower peak stresses), decreased micro-scale elemental segregation (as seen by improved EDS uniformity), a finer and more uniform grain structure, and improved mechanical performance (e.g., higher yield strength and better defect tolerance).
generation.baseline: AlCrFeNiSi components manufactured by conventional additive manufacturing using a constant laser power profile.
generation.boundary: Valid for laser additive manufacturing processes (such as LPBF or DED) operating within typical energy density and processing temperature ranges for AlCrFeNiSi. Effects may vary for significantly different build geometries or when using powders with markedly different characteristics.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal modulation frequency and power amplitude are not yet known; this study extrapolates the benefits observed in reducing hot cracking in CrFeNiTi alloys (PMC9698306) and the role of laser power in controlling segregation (PMC12525219) to cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi. Quantitative improvement levels are uncertain until experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples using additive manufacturing under otherwise identical conditions: one set using conventional constant laser power and the other with high-frequency laser power modulation. Characterize both groups for residual stress, microstructural uniformity, elemental segregation, and mechanical properties.
measurements: Residual stress measurements (e.g., X-ray diffraction stress analysis or hole-drilling method)
Microstructural analysis via EBSD and SEM to assess grain size and defect densities
Mechanical testing for yield strength, tensile strength, and ductility
Defect density evaluation using high-resolution micro-CT or SEM imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples produced with high-frequency laser power modulation do not statistically exhibit reduced residual stresses, decreased elemental segregation, a refined microstructure, and improved mechanical properties compared to the constant power baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: By combining the response data for each group presented in Table 10 with the radar plot shown in Figure 13, the results indicate that the optimized parameter group demonstrates superior cladding layer geometry quality, characterized by moderate width and height, clear contours, a low dilution rate, and good forming continuity. In contrast, the initial group exhibited a wide but inadequately high cladding layer, likely due to insufficient powder melting resulting from low laser power. Although the standard group displayed moderate width, it also showed a high dilution rate, indicative of excessive substrate melting. The radar plot further illustrates the balanced performance of the optimized group in terms of width, height, and dilution rate, culminating in an overall geometrical profile that is closer to the ideal. In terms of elemental segregation, the optimized group demonstrated the most uniform distribution of major elements, including Al, Cr, and Fe, with minimal segregation. cited_evidence.text: Microsections were prepared and throughout the initial investigation, samples with noteworthy lack of fusion defects or significant keyhole porosity were ruled out. In addition to these defects, large horizontal cracks were seen as critical defects, disrupting the fabrication process due to the deterioration of the thermal conductivity towards the substrate plate, as well as the possible detachment of entire sections. Therefore, the initial set of 16 samples was reduced to four samples, which exhibited large defect-free sections, and the defects present were predominantly limited to vertical cracking (Figure 6). Vertical cracks were expected due to the absence of preheating (substrate plate preheating was not employed), coupled with the larger than usual layer thickness. Raising the build space temperature to lower cooling rates and thermal gradients is the most common approach to minimize cracking. New research also suggests that high-frequency laser power modulation is a suitable approach to prevent cracking [].
